raw: Act 5, Scene 3 — A churchyard; in it a Monument belonging to the Capulets
Enter Paris, and his Page bearing flowers and a torch.

gemma4_gloss.en: Paris enters.
His Page carries flowers and a torch.

speaker: PARIS
raw:
Give me thy torch, boy. Hence and stand aloof.
Yet put it out, for I would not be seen.
Under yond yew tree lay thee all along,
Holding thy ear close to the hollow ground;
So shall no foot upon the churchyard tread,
Being loose, unfirm, with digging up of graves,
But thou shalt hear it. Whistle then to me,
As signal that thou hear’st something approach.
Give me those flowers. Do as I bid thee, go.

gemma4_gloss.en: Give me your torch, boy.
Go away and stand far apart.
Put it out because I do not want to be seen.
Lie under that yew tree all the time.
Hold your ear close to the ground.
No foot will walk in this churchyard.
The ground is loose and not firm.
Digging up graves makes it unstable.
But you will hear it if something moves.
Whistle to me then.
Whistle as a signal that you hear something coming.
Give me those flowers.
Do what I tell you and go.

speaker: PAGE
raw:
I am almost afraid to stand alone
Here in the churchyard; yet I will adventure.

gemma4_gloss.en: I am almost afraid to stand alone here in the churchyard.
Still, I will take the risk.

raw: Retires.

gemma4_gloss.en: The page leaves.

speaker: PARIS
raw:
Sweet flower, with flowers thy bridal bed I strew.
O woe, thy canopy is dust and stones,
Which with sweet water nightly I will dew,
Or wanting that, with tears distill’d by moans.
The obsequies that I for thee will keep,
Nightly shall be to strew thy grave and weep.

gemma4_gloss.en: Sweet flower, I scatter flowers on your wedding bed.
Oh woe, your canopy is only dust and stones.
I will water it with sweet water every night.
If I lack that, I will use tears from my crying.
The ceremonies I will keep for you will be to scatter flowers on your grave and weep every night.

raw: The Page whistles.

gemma4_gloss.en: The Page whistles.

speaker: PARIS
raw:
The boy gives warning something doth approach.
What cursed foot wanders this way tonight,
To cross my obsequies and true love’s rite?
What, with a torch! Muffle me, night, awhile.

gemma4_gloss.en: The boy signals that something is coming.
What cursed foot wanders this way tonight?
It interrupts my prayers and the ceremony of true love.
What? It has a torch!
Night, hide me for a while.

raw: Retires.

gemma4_gloss.en: Paris leaves.

raw: Enter Romeo and Balthasar with a torch, mattock, &c.

gemma4_gloss.en: Romeo and Balthasar enter with a torch and a tool.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Give me that mattock and the wrenching iron.
Hold, take this letter; early in the morning
See thou deliver it to my lord and father.
Give me the light; upon thy life I charge thee,
Whate’er thou hear’st or seest, stand all aloof
And do not interrupt me in my course.
Why I descend into this bed of death
Is partly to behold my lady’s face,
But chiefly to take thence from her dead finger
A precious ring, a ring that I must use
In dear employment. Therefore hence, be gone.
But if thou jealous dost return to pry
In what I further shall intend to do,
By heaven I will tear thee joint by joint,
And strew this hungry churchyard with thy limbs.
The time and my intents are savage-wild;
More fierce and more inexorable far
Than empty tigers or the roaring sea.

gemma4_gloss.en: Give me that tool and the iron bar.
Wait, take this letter.
Deliver it to my lord and father early in the morning.
Give me the light.
I charge you on your life.
Whatever you hear or see, stay away.
Do not stop me from what I am doing.
I go into this bed of death partly to see my lady's face.
But mostly I want to take a precious ring from her dead finger.
I must use this ring for an important task.
Therefore, go away now.
If you are curious and try to find out what I plan to do next, I swear by heaven that I will tear you apart.
I will scatter your body parts across this hungry churchyard.
The time and my plans are wild.
They are much more fierce and unstoppable than tigers or the roaring sea.

speaker: BALTHASAR
raw: I will be gone, sir, and not trouble you.

gemma4_gloss.en: I will leave now, sir, and not bother you.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
So shalt thou show me friendship. Take thou that.
Live, and be prosperous, and farewell, good fellow.

gemma4_gloss.en: That is how you show me friendship.
Take that.
Live and be successful, and goodbye, good fellow.

speaker: BALTHASAR
raw:
For all this same, I’ll hide me hereabout.
His looks I fear, and his intents I doubt.

gemma4_gloss.en: I will hide nearby for all these reasons.

raw: Retires

gemma4_gloss.en: Balthasar leaves.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Thou detestable maw, thou womb of death,
Gorg’d with the dearest morsel of the earth,
Thus I enforce thy rotten jaws to open,

raw: Breaking open the door of the monument.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: And in despite, I’ll cram thee with more food.

speaker: PARIS
raw:
This is that banish’d haughty Montague
That murder’d my love’s cousin,—with which grief,
It is supposed, the fair creature died,—
And here is come to do some villainous shame
To the dead bodies. I will apprehend him.

raw: Advances.

speaker: PARIS
raw:
Stop thy unhallow’d toil, vile Montague.
Can vengeance be pursu’d further than death?
Condemned villain, I do apprehend thee.
Obey, and go with me, for thou must die.

I must indeed; and therefore came I hither.
Good gentle youth, tempt not a desperate man.
Fly hence and leave me. Think upon these gone;
Let them affright thee. I beseech thee, youth,
Put not another sin upon my head
By urging me to fury. O be gone.
By heaven I love thee better than myself;
For I come hither arm’d against myself.
Stay not, be gone, live, and hereafter say,
A madman’s mercy bid thee run away.

speaker: PARIS

I do defy thy conjuration,
And apprehend thee for a felon here.

If thou be merciful,
Open the tomb, lay me with Juliet.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
In faith, I will. Let me peruse this face.
Mercutio’s kinsman, noble County Paris!
What said my man, when my betossed soul
Did not attend him as we rode? I think
He told me Paris should have married Juliet.
Said he not so? Or did I dream it so?
Or am I mad, hearing him talk of Juliet,
To think it was so? O, give me thy hand,
One writ with me in sour misfortune’s book.
I’ll bury thee in a triumphant grave.
A grave? O no, a lantern, slaught’red youth,
For here lies Juliet, and her beauty makes
This vault a feasting presence full of light.
Death, lie thou there, by a dead man interr’d.

gemma4_gloss.en: I will do that.
Let me look at this face.
Mercutio's relative, the noble County Paris!
What did my man say when my lost soul did not listen to him while we rode?
I think he told me Paris should have married Juliet.
Did he not say that?
Or did I dream it?
Or am I mad for hearing him talk of Juliet and thinking it was true?
Oh, give me your hand.
It is written with me in the book of bad luck.
I will bury you in a triumphant grave.
A grave? Oh no, a lantern.
You are a slaughtered youth.
Juliet lies here.
Her beauty makes this vault a feast full of light.
Death, stay there, buried by a dead man.

raw: Laying Paris in the monument.

gemma4_gloss.en: Romeo is laying Paris in the monument.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
How oft when men are at the point of death
Have they been merry! Which their keepers call
A lightning before death. O, how may I
Call this a lightning? O my love, my wife,
Death that hath suck’d the honey of thy breath,
Hath had no power yet upon thy beauty.
Thou art not conquer’d. Beauty’s ensign yet
Is crimson in thy lips and in thy cheeks,
And death’s pale flag is not advanced there.
Tybalt, liest thou there in thy bloody sheet?
O, what more favour can I do to thee
Than with that hand that cut thy youth in twain
To sunder his that was thine enemy?
Forgive me, cousin. Ah, dear Juliet,
Why art thou yet so fair? Shall I believe
That unsubstantial death is amorous;
And that the lean abhorred monster keeps
Thee here in dark to be his paramour?
For fear of that I still will stay with thee,
And never from this palace of dim night
Depart again. Here, here will I remain
With worms that are thy chambermaids. O, here
Will I set up my everlasting rest;
And shake the yoke of inauspicious stars
From this world-wearied flesh. Eyes, look your last.
Arms, take your last embrace! And, lips, O you
The doors of breath, seal with a righteous kiss
A dateless bargain to engrossing death.
Come, bitter conduct, come, unsavoury guide.
Thou desperate pilot, now at once run on
The dashing rocks thy sea-sick weary bark.
Here’s to my love!

gemma4_gloss.en: How often have men been happy at the moment of death!
Their keepers call this a flash before death.
Oh, how can I call this a flash?
Oh my love, my wife, death has taken the honey from your breath.
But death has no power over your beauty yet.
You are not conquered.
The sign of beauty is still red in your lips and cheeks.
Death's pale flag is not there.
Tybalt, do you lie there in your bloody sheet?
Oh, what more can I do for you?
I will use the hand that cut your life in two to separate his hand from yours.
Forgive me, cousin.
Ah, dear Juliet, why are you still so beautiful?
Should I believe that weak death is in love?
And that the thin, hated monster keeps you here in the dark as his lover?
Because of that fear, I will stay with you.
I will never leave this palace of dark night.
Here, I will stay with the worms that are your maids.
Oh, here I will set up my forever rest.
I will shake the weight of unlucky stars from this tired body.
Eyes, look for the last time.
Arms, give your last embrace!
And lips, oh you doors of breath, seal with a holy kiss a deal with death that never ends.
Come, bitter journey, come, unpleasant guide.
You desperate pilot, now sail at once on the rocks.
Your sea-sick weary boat is hitting them.
Here is to my love!

raw: Drinks.

gemma4_gloss.en: Romeo drinks.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
O true apothecary!
Thy drugs are quick. Thus with a kiss I die.

gemma4_gloss.en: Oh, true apothecary!
Your drugs work quickly.
I die with a kiss.

gemma4_gloss.en: Romeo dies.

raw:

Have my old feet stumbled at graves? Who’s there?
Who is it that consorts, so late, the dead?

How many times tonight have my old feet tripped over graves?
Who is there?

raw: Romeo.

raw: Romeo!

Let luck wait for patience.
Bring out the people involved in this suspicion.

speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
raw:
I am the greatest, able to do least,
Yet most suspected, as the time and place
Doth make against me, of this direful murder.
And here I stand, both to impeach and purge
Myself condemned and myself excus’d.

gemma4_gloss.en: I am a man of high status, but I can do very little.
However, I am the most suspected person because of the time and place of this terrible murder.
I stand here both to accuse others and to defend myself.

speaker: PRINCE
raw: Then say at once what thou dost know in this.

gemma4_gloss.en: Then tell me at once what you know about this.

speaker: FRIAR LAWRENCE
raw:
I will be brief, for my short date of breath
Is not so long as is a tedious tale.
Romeo, there dead, was husband to that Juliet,
And she, there dead, that Romeo’s faithful wife.
I married them; and their stol’n marriage day
Was Tybalt’s doomsday, whose untimely death
Banish’d the new-made bridegroom from this city;
For whom, and not for Tybalt, Juliet pin’d.
You, to remove that siege of grief from her,
Betroth’d, and would have married her perforce
To County Paris. Then comes she to me,
And with wild looks, bid me devise some means
To rid her from this second marriage,
Or in my cell there would she kill herself.
Then gave I her, so tutored by my art,
A sleeping potion, which so took effect
As I intended, for it wrought on her
The form of death. Meantime I writ to Romeo
That he should hither come as this dire night
To help to take her from her borrow’d grave,
Being the time the potion’s force should cease.
But he which bore my letter, Friar John,
Was stay’d by accident; and yesternight
Return’d my letter back. Then all alone
At the prefixed hour of her waking
Came I to take her from her kindred’s vault,
Meaning to keep her closely at my cell
Till I conveniently could send to Romeo.
But when I came, some minute ere the time
Of her awaking, here untimely lay
The noble Paris and true Romeo dead.
She wakes; and I entreated her come forth
And bear this work of heaven with patience.
But then a noise did scare me from the tomb;
And she, too desperate, would not go with me,
But, as it seems, did violence on herself.
All this I know; and to the marriage
Her Nurse is privy. And if ought in this
Miscarried by my fault, let my old life
Be sacrific’d, some hour before his time,
Unto the rigour of severest law.

gemma4_gloss.en: I will be brief.
My short life is not long enough for a boring story.
Romeo, dead there, was the husband of that Juliet.
And she, dead there, was Romeo's faithful wife.
I married them.
Their secret wedding day was Tybalt's last day.
His early death forced the new groom to leave this city.
She loved him, not Tybalt.
You promised her to remove her sadness.
You betrothed her and wanted to marry her to County Paris.
Then she came to me.
With a wild look, she asked me to find a way to stop this second marriage.
She said she would kill herself in my cell if I did not help.
Then I gave her a sleeping potion as I had taught her.
It worked exactly as I planned.
It made her look like death.
Meanwhile, I wrote to Romeo.
I told him to come here tonight.
He was to take her from her borrowed grave.
He was to arrive when the potion's power ended.
But Friar John, who carried my letter, was stopped by an accident.
He returned my letter last night.
Then I came alone at the planned time.
I came to take her from her family's vault.
I planned to keep her in my cell until I could send word to Romeo.
But when I arrived, just before she woke up, the noble Paris and true Romeo lay here dead.
She wakes now.
I asked her to come out.
I told her to accept this act of heaven with patience.
But then a noise scared me away from the tomb.
She was desperate and would not go with me.
It seems she hurt herself.
I know all of this.
Her Nurse knows about the marriage.
If anything went wrong because of my fault, let my old life be sacrificed to the harshest law.
Let it happen sooner than its time.

speaker: PRINCE
raw:
We still have known thee for a holy man.
Where’s Romeo’s man? What can he say to this?

gemma4_gloss.en: We have always known you as a holy man.
Where is Romeo's man?
What can he say about this?

speaker: BALTHASAR
raw:
I brought my master news of Juliet’s death,
And then in post he came from Mantua
To this same place, to this same monument.
This letter he early bid me give his father,
And threaten’d me with death, going in the vault,
If I departed not, and left him there.

gemma4_gloss.en: I brought my master news of Juliet's death.
Then he came from Mantua to this place.
He came to this same monument.
He told me to give this letter to his father early.
He threatened me with death if I left him alone in the vault.
He told me not to leave him there.

speaker: PRINCE
raw:
Give me the letter, I will look on it.
Where is the County’s Page that rais’d the watch?
Sirrah, what made your master in this place?

gemma4_gloss.en: Give me the letter. I will look at it.
Where is the County's Page who kept watch?
You there, why did your master come to this place?

speaker: PAGE
raw:
He came with flowers to strew his lady’s grave,
And bid me stand aloof, and so I did.
Anon comes one with light to ope the tomb,
And by and by my master drew on him,
And then I ran away to call the watch.

gemma4_gloss.en: He came with flowers to scatter on his lady's grave.
He told me to stand away, and I did so.
Someone is coming soon with a light to open the tomb.
In a moment, my master moved toward him.
Then I ran away to call the guards.
I am coming right away.

speaker: PRINCE
raw:
This letter doth make good the Friar’s words,
Their course of love, the tidings of her death.
And here he writes that he did buy a poison
Of a poor ’pothecary, and therewithal
Came to this vault to die, and lie with Juliet.
Where be these enemies? Capulet, Montague,
See what a scourge is laid upon your hate,
That heaven finds means to kill your joys with love!
And I, for winking at your discords too,
Have lost a brace of kinsmen. All are punish’d.

gemma4_gloss.en: This letter confirms the Friar's words.
It tells of their love and the news of her death.
He writes here that he bought poison from a poor medicine seller.
He came to this vault to die and lie with Juliet.
Where are these enemies? Capulet, Montague.
Look at what a punishment is placed on your hatred.
Heaven found a way to kill your joys with love!
And I, for ignoring your fights, have lost two relatives.
All are punished.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
O brother Montague, give me thy hand.
This is my daughter’s jointure, for no more
Can I demand.

gemma4_gloss.en: Oh brother Montague, give me your hand.
This is my daughter's jointure.
I can demand no more.

speaker: MONTAGUE
raw:
But I can give thee more,
For I will raise her statue in pure gold,
That whiles Verona by that name is known,
There shall no figure at such rate be set
As that of true and faithful Juliet.

gemma4_gloss.en: But I can give you more.
I will make her statue out of pure gold.
As long as Verona is known by that name, no other statue will be so valuable.
No figure will be set as great as the one of true and faithful Juliet.

speaker: CAPULET
raw:
As rich shall Romeo’s by his lady’s lie,
Poor sacrifices of our enmity.

gemma4_gloss.en: Romeo's shall be just as rich as his lady's.
They are poor sacrifices of our hatred.

speaker: PRINCE
raw:
A glooming peace this morning with it brings;
The sun for sorrow will not show his head.
Go hence, to have more talk of these sad things.
Some shall be pardon’d, and some punished,
For never was a story of more woe
Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.

gemma4_gloss.en: This morning brings a gloomy peace.
The sun will not show its face because of the sadness.
Go away to talk more about these sad things.
Some will be pardoned, and some punished.
No story was ever sadder than this story of Juliet and her Romeo.

raw: Exeunt.
